description: The Mughal Empire ruled a large part of the Indian subcontinent from 1526 to 1857. This period is renowned for its robust military system, administrative innovations, and rich cultural, architectural, and literary heritage.

sections.title: Early Mughals: Babur and Humayun
sections.description: The foundation and early struggles of the Mughal Empire in India.

key_concepts.explanation: A military strategy adopted by Babur that involved dividing the army to flank the enemy (Tulughma) and using a cart-based artillery system (Araba).

historical_events.significance: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, effectively ending the Delhi Sultanate and laying the foundation of the Mughal Empire.
Babur defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar, cementing Mughal dominance in North India.
Sher Shah Suri decisively defeated Humayun, forcing him into exile and temporarily establishing the Suri Empire.
Humayun defeated Sikandar Shah Suri, re-establishing Mughal rule in India.

sections.title: Era of Akbar: Expansion and Consolidation
sections.description: Akbar's reign is considered the Golden Age of the Mughal Empire, marked by massive territorial expansion and administrative reforms.

key_concepts.explanation: A military and civil administrative system introduced by Akbar where officers were granted a rank (Mansab) determined by 'Zat' (personal rank/salary) and 'Sawar' (number of cavalrymen maintained).
A land revenue system developed by Raja Todar Mal, based on the average crop yield and prices over the preceding 10 years.
A syncretic religious movement propounded by Akbar in 1582, blending moral and ethical principles of major religions to promote tolerance.

historical_events.significance: The Mughal army, led by Bairam Khan, defeated Hemu Vikramaditya, securing the throne for young Akbar.
An inconclusive but highly significant battle between the Mughal forces (led by Raja Man Singh) and Maharana Pratap of Mewar.

important_facts.fact: Akbar commissioned the construction of the 'Ibadat Khana' (House of Worship) at Fatehpur Sikri to host religious and philosophical debates.

sections.title: Jahangir and Shah Jahan: Art and Architecture
sections.description: During this period, Mughal painting and architecture reached their absolute zenith.

historical_events.significance: The English ambassador obtained a royal farman (decree) from Jahangir to establish factories and trade in India.

key_associations.extra_info: Ustad Mansoor (specialist in flora/fauna) and Abul Hasan were prominent painters in his court.
Marked by the construction of the Taj Mahal, Red Fort, and Jama Masjid using white marble and red sandstone.
A famous jeweled throne that originally contained the legendary Koh-i-Noor diamond.

sections.title: Aurangzeb and the Decline of the Empire
sections.description: Aurangzeb's orthodox policies and the subsequent weak successors led to the eventual collapse of the empire.

key_concepts.explanation: Aurangzeb's exhausting, decades-long military campaign in South India against the Marathas and Deccan Sultanates, which drained the Mughal treasury.

historical_events.significance: Aurangzeb defeated his brother Dara Shikoh at the Battle of Samugarh to usurp the Mughal throne.
Aurangzeb re-imposed the Jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims), reversing Akbar's policy and alienating Hindu subjects.
His death in Ahmednagar marked the beginning of the rapid decline of the Mughal Empire.

important_facts.fact: Aurangzeb was often referred to as 'Zinda Pir' (Living Saint) due to his simple and austere lifestyle.
The last Mughal Emperor was Bahadur Shah II (Zafar), who was exiled to Rangoon by the British after the Revolt of 1857.

sections.title: Mughal Administration and Literature
sections.description: Key structural elements of the Mughal administration and monumental literary works produced during the era.

key_concepts.explanation: The head of the military department and intelligence, who was also responsible for paying the Mansabdars.
The finance minister or chief revenue officer of the empire, responsible for all income and expenditures.

key_associations.extra_info: Babur's autobiography, originally written in his native Chagatai Turkic language.
A biography of Humayun written by his half-sister, providing deep insights into the Mughal harem.
A detailed, multi-volume Persian document recording the history of Akbar's reign and his administration.

important_facts.fact: The official court language of the Mughal Empire was Persian.
